title: How to Choose a Dropshipping Partner Like Zendrop
excerpt: Choosing a dropshipping supplier is a shortlist exercise against four numbers: landed cost, shipping time, automation, and support. A framework that turns the decision into a scored comparison.
body: Choosing a dropshipping supplier is not a single yes-or-no decision; it is a shortlist exercise against the four numbers that decide whether your store makes money: landed cost per unit, shipping time to your buyers, how much automation the workflow allows, and what happens when something goes wrong. Using a tool like Zendrop as a working example, this framework walks through the four checks in the order they should run, so the supplier decision becomes a scored comparison instead of a gut call.

Start with the landed cost per unit, not the catalog price. Add the supplier cost, the shipping cost to your customer's country, and any membership fee spread across your expected volume. A supplier that looks five dollars cheaper per item can lose that advantage on a two-dollar shipping premium or a membership fee on a store selling thirty units a month. The right number to write down is the all-in cost for your real order sizes, because that is what your retail margin is built on.

Then check shipping time to the markets you actually sell into. Dropshipping margins are decided by speed more than any other variable, since a ten-day wait is a refund and a five-star review at the same time. The clean way to measure is to place a small test order to each target country and time it, rather than trusting the estimated range on a product page. A partner with domestic or nearby warehouses for your main market changes the math completely, because it turns a thirty-day promise into a five-day one.

Third, score the automation surface. The part of dropshipping that eats your week is order entry, tracking updates, and inventory syncing, and a tool that handles those in one click is worth more than a marginally cheaper supplier. Look for one-click import of products with your own pricing, automatic order fulfillment from your store, and tracking that flows back to the customer without manual steps. Zendrop is built around this workflow, and its product page at /tool/zendrop in the directory explains the plan structure, so the automation check is a page view rather than a demo cycle.

Fourth, stress the support path before you need it. Ask how order issues, quality complaints, and missing items are handled, and whether there is real human support or only a ticket system. Ship a cheap product to yourself and deliberately report a problem to see how fast the resolution is and whether you can reach a human. A supplier that answers in minutes during your test will protect you during a busy season; one that answers in days will turn your own reviews into negative ones.

Score each candidate on the four checks, weigh shipping time and landed cost more heavily for a new store, and pick the one that wins the weighted total rather than the lowest price. Re-run the scorecard every quarter, because shipping lanes, fees, and warehouse coverage all drift. The DTCwise dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist of suppliers and tools with ratings and pricing, so the next supplier decision is a comparison you can finish in an afternoon.
